NDT inspection software for reporting: what Atlantis does

Atlantis NDT reporting software takes an inspection from the technician's tablet to a signed report in the client's hands. Technicians capture readings, weld lines and photos in a field app that works offline. Each report follows a method-specific template in your own format. It then moves through review and approval with recorded signatures, and is issued to the client. It runs as the NDT Reports app in Atlantis NDT ERP, so every report stays tied to its job, technician and instrument.

This section covers what the software does at each stage, how a shop moves off Word and Excel, and how to evaluate any NDT reporting software, ours included. For a side-by-side view of the market, see the NDT reporting software comparison for 2026. To see it on your own report formats, book a reporting demo.

From field reading to client report, stage by stage

Every report follows the same five stages. They are simple on purpose. Anyone in the office can see where a report is and who is holding it.

StageWhat happensWho actsWhat the record holds
DraftThe report is opened against the job, usually from the work order, with job references already filled inOffice or technicianWork order, client request number, contract and drawing references
In progressReadings, weld lines, defects and photos are captured, online or offlineTechnician (Level I or II)Method data, instrument and probes issued, photos, technician signature
ReviewThe reviewer checks technique, coverage, sizing and the acceptance standard, then approves or sends backLevel II or Level III reviewerReviewer comments and signature
ApprovedThe approver signs. On client and code work, a third-party or authorized inspector's name and signature can be recorded tooApprover, and witness inspector where usedApprover signature, inspector name and signature
SentThe report goes out in your template, and the record shows it has left the buildingOfficeIssue date and output file

Every report ends with one of three results: acceptable, not acceptable, or acceptable with remarks. The third option matters. It lets a Level II record a condition the client should know about without failing the item, and it shows clearly on the report rather than in a comment nobody reads.

Because stages are tracked, the questions that used to need a phone call get answered on screen. Which reports from last week's turnaround are still in review? Which are approved but not sent? Which technician has three drafts open?

Field capture and offline use

Tank farms, pipe racks, ship holds and pipeline spreads share one thing: bad signal. A reporting tool that needs a live connection gets abandoned on day one, and the notebook comes back out.

The field app is an installable web app. You add it to a tablet, phone or laptop like any other app, and it works offline. Drafts and photos are stored on the device and sync when a connection returns. On the device, the technician gets:

  • Their assigned jobs. The app opens on the jobs dispatched to that technician, not a blank form.
  • Their issued equipment. The instrument and probes on the report come from what was actually issued to that person, by serial number. That removes a common audit finding: an instrument named on a report that was in the calibration lab that day.
  • A method picker. The right report type and fields open for the method.
  • Photo capture straight into the report.
  • An on-screen signature.
  • A PDF preview before submitting, so the technician sees what the reviewer and client will see.

The software covers 17 report types, each with its own fields and its own numbering sequence: UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ECT, IRIS, PAUT, MFL, TOFD, PWHT, PMI, hardness, UT thickness, ferrite, holiday and coating, and computed radiography. A UT report holds a probe calibration table and indications with type and orientation. An RT report holds source, technique and IQI type and placement. A PAUT report holds focal laws. UT thickness readings are recorded by direction. Separate numbering per method means your UT and RT sequences never collide.

A practical tip from rollouts: test offline before go-live, on the actual tablets, in the worst-signal location you work. Put the device in airplane mode, write a full report with photos, then reconnect and check it arrived complete.

Code templates and your own report formats

Clients care about two things in a report's format. Does it contain what the governing code requires, and does it look like what they are used to receiving? The software handles both.

  • Your templates, not ours. Company templates can be Word, Excel, PDF or HTML, with your logo, header and footer. If a client expects an Excel-format report, the software fills the Excel template by mapping report fields to cells. The layout stays familiar and the re-typing stops.
  • Versioned templates. When a client changes its required format mid-contract, you add a new version instead of overwriting the old one. You keep a record of which format was in use and when.
  • Code-aligned content. Templates are built for the codes your clients cite, such as ASME Section V, AWS D1.1, API 1104 and API 510, 570 and 653 work. Each report records the procedure reference and the code or standard used for acceptance.
  • Traceable references. Work order, client request number, contract and drawing numbers, and the WPS number for weld inspections are held as fields, not typed into a header.
  • Marine mode. For class surveys and ship repair, a vessel cover page is added and the PDF merges the classification-society certificate, the inspector's Level II certificate and the instrument's calibration certificate. Photos are laid out two to a page so a thickness survey stays readable.

The reason this matters is the audit, not the look. A year after the job, when a client queries a result, the report itself tells them which procedure and which standard were applied. For how templates should be structured by method and by code, read NDT report templates by method and by code.

Review, sign-off and the client portal

Signatures are captured for the inspector, the reviewer and the approver, so the PDF shows who did what. Who may create, review and approve is set by role during implementation, in line with your written practice. If your written practice does not yet say who may sign what, fix that first. An ASNT Level III can write it into your procedures before the software is configured. See ASNT Level III consulting services.

Because reporting sits in the same ERP as personnel records, technician certifications, levels and expiry dates are held on each person's NDT profile, and timesheets warn when a technician's certificate is not valid. The certification tracking page explains that link.

Once approved, reports can be shared through a client portal. Each client contact logs in and sees their own reports, rather than waiting for an email. How the portal is organised, for example by job, by site or by equipment tag, is agreed during implementation. Ask for it to be organised the way your client searches. A reliability engineer looks for a vessel or a line, not a job number. For what a client portal for inspection reports needs to do, read inspection report portals and revision control.

Some asset owners also want to see where each finding sits on the asset. That is a separate Atlantis product, Digital Twin reporting, which places inspection data on 3D assets. The reporting software produces the signed record. The digital twin gives the spatial view. You can start with one and add the other. See Digital Twin reporting.

Moving off Word and Excel: a step-by-step plan

Most shops that call us run reports in Word and Excel. The templates have been edited by several people over the years. Readings go from a notebook or clipboard into the office, get re-typed, get printed for the Level III, then go to the client as a PDF days later. Every hand-off is a chance to transpose a reading or copy last week's probe serial. Here is how the move usually runs.

  1. Collect your current reports. One recent report per method, plus the formats your three biggest clients insist on. This is the real requirement, more than any feature list.
  2. Decide what stays the same. Usually the client-facing layout stays. What changes is where the data comes from.
  3. Load templates. Your Word, Excel or PDF layouts are loaded as versioned templates, with Excel fields mapped to cells where you use Excel.
  4. Set numbering and roles. Report numbering per method follows your convention. Inspector, reviewer and approver roles are assigned to match your written practice.
  5. Connect jobs, people and equipment. Technicians, instruments and probes are loaded so the field app shows the right assignments and issued equipment.
  6. Roll out the field app. Technicians install it and complete one offline job with us watching.
  7. Run one method first. Start with the method that produces the most reports, often UT thickness or VT. Keep Word as the fallback for the other methods for a short period.
  8. Go live and adjust. The first weeks of real reports surface small template changes. Those are part of setup, not change orders.
  9. Retire the old templates. Remove them from the shared drive once each method is live, or someone will keep using them.

Old reports do not need to be converted. Keep the archive as it is, and start structured records from go-live. Atlantis ERP implementation typically takes 2-4 weeks, and a reporting rollout follows the same steps. For where spreadsheets break down in more detail, see NDT reporting software vs Excel.

Who it fits

  • Small NDT service companies. A handful of technicians, one office person and a Level II doing review at night. Start with reporting and certificates and add other ERP apps later, or never. Pricing is quote on request and follows the number of users and apps you take, so a small shop does not pay for a large company's system.
  • Mid-size contractors with several crews. The main gain is visibility: what is stuck in review across all crews, and which jobs have no report yet.
  • Turnaround-heavy contractors. When hundreds of reports arrive in a few days, a review queue with clear stages is what lets the Level III keep up.
  • Marine inspection companies and ship repair yards. Marine mode removes the work of assembling certificate packs by hand.
  • Owner-operator inspection teams. In-house crews at plants use the same workflow so their records match those of their contractors.

Gulf Coast users can see local context on the Houston and New Orleans pages, and midcontinent pipeline users on the Tulsa page.

How to evaluate NDT reporting software

Feature lists look alike. Demos look alike too, because vendors show their best report type on fast Wi-Fi. Use your own reports and your own conditions instead. These are the tests we would run on any vendor, including us.

CriterionWhat to test in the demoWhy it matters
Offline captureAirplane mode, a full report with photos, then reconnectIf it fails offline, technicians go back to paper
Method depthYour hardest method, for example PAUT or RT, not just UT thicknessGeneric forms push method data into free text
Your formatsBring a client's required template and ask to see it producedClients will not change their format for your software
Code referencesDoes the report record the procedure and acceptance standard as fields?Auditors and client inspectors check these first
Review and sign-offSend a report back from review, then approve it, and look at the recordShows whether signatures and comments are traceable
Equipment traceabilityIs the instrument on the report linked to its calibration record?Removes the out-of-calibration instrument finding
PersonnelCan it show a technician's certification status?Clients ask who did the work and whether they were certified
Client deliveryLog in as a client contact and find a reportA portal clients cannot search becomes an email inbox again
Connection to jobs and invoicingFollow a report back to its work order and forward to the invoiceA stand-alone report tool means re-typing job data
ExitAsk how you get your data and PDFs out if you leaveRecords outlive software contracts

Frequently asked questions

What is NDT inspection software?

It is software that records NDT inspection data and produces the inspection report, from field capture through review and approval to the client. Some products stop at the report. Atlantis reporting runs inside Atlantis NDT ERP, so the report stays linked to the job, the technician and the instrument.

Is there affordable NDT reporting software for small businesses?

Yes. A small shop can start with reporting and certificates only and add other apps later. Pricing is quote on request, based on users and the apps you take, so you pay for the scope you use.

Does it work offline on a tablet or laptop?

Yes. The field app is an installable web app that runs on tablets, phones and laptops. Drafts and photos are stored on the device and sync when a connection returns.

Can we keep our own report templates?

Yes. Your Word, Excel, PDF or HTML layouts are loaded as versioned templates. Excel templates are filled by mapping report fields to cells, so clients receive the format they already know.

Which NDT methods does the reporting software cover?

Seventeen report types: UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ECT, IRIS, PAUT, MFL, TOFD, PWHT, PMI, hardness, UT thickness, ferrite, holiday and coating, and computed radiography. Each has its own fields and numbering.

How does review and sign-off work?

Reports move from draft to in progress, review, approved and sent. Inspector, reviewer and approver signatures are captured, and a third-party or authorized inspector's name and signature can be recorded. Roles follow your written practice.

Can our clients get reports through a portal?

Yes. Approved reports can be shared through a client portal where each client contact sees their own reports. How it is organised is agreed during implementation.

How long does it take to move off Word and Excel?

Atlantis ERP implementation typically takes 2-4 weeks. Most shops go live one method at a time, starting with the method that produces the most reports.
